nameStory: Creeping speedwell gets its name from its low-growing, spreading habit that creeps along the ground. The "speedwell" part comes from an old English farewell blessing meaning "may you prosper" or "Godspeed," given to this plant because it was thought to bring good luck to travelers who carried it.
description: Creeping speedwell is a low-growing perennial that spreads along the ground with trailing stems. It forms a mat-like carpet rarely more than a few inches tall, making it popular in rock gardens and as ground cover. The plant stays green most of the year (semi-evergreen) and produces cheerful blue flowers in spring. Its simple leaves are arranged alternately along creeping stems that root as they spread.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, bright blue flowers with four petals that appear in spring, creating a carpet of blue blooms across the creeping mat

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low, spreading mat that creeps along the ground, with stems that root where they touch soil

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, small leaves arranged alternately along the stems, staying green through most of the winter

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Trailing stems that feel somewhat soft and bend easily, spreading outward from the center to form colonies

habitat: Creeping speedwell thrives in well-drained soils in sunny, sheltered locations throughout New England. You'll often find it in rock gardens, alpine gardens, or gravelly areas where drainage is excellent. It prefers full sun but needs some protection from harsh winter winds.

seasonality.spring: The main show begins with bright blue flowers covering the mat-like plant, making it easily spotted and identified.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the green mat continues to spread, with stems rooting as they creep across the ground.
seasonality.fall: The semi-evergreen foliage remains green, though growth slows as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Most leaves stay green through winter in sheltered spots, making it one of the few speedwells you can identify year-round.

funFact: The cultivar 'Georgia Blue' has won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, making this humble creeping plant officially recognized as one of the world's most outstanding garden plants!
confusionNotes: With 18 different speedwell species in New England, identification can be tricky! Creeping speedwell's mat-forming, semi-evergreen habit sets it apart from most others. Remember: "creeping and keeping green" - it creeps along the ground and keeps its leaves green through winter, unlike most speedwells that die back completely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "creeping speedwell" in common usage, botanists sometimes list this plant under different scientific names (Veronica peduncularis vs. Veronica umbrosa), which can cause confusion when looking it up in different field guides or websites.
compareHints: Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats. While bird's-eye speedwell and thyme-leaved speedwell also creep somewhat, they don't form the dense, semi-evergreen carpets that this species creates. Most other speedwells in our region grow more upright rather than forming flat mats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
